canonicalExplanation.summary: A **virtual** function is chosen at **run time** based on the object's **actual (dynamic) type**, when it's called **through a base reference or pointer**. Without `virtual`, a call through `Shape&` always runs Shape's version. Mark overrides with **`override`** so the compiler catches signature typos. A **pure virtual** function (`= 0`) makes the class **abstract**: an interface you can't instantiate. And any base class you'll `delete` through a base pointer (for example via `unique_ptr<Shape>`) needs a **virtual destructor**, or the derived part's destructor never runs.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner stores shapes in `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Shape>>` and calls draw() on each. Every shape prints "shape", because Shape::draw wasn't virtual. After fixing that, a Circle holding a file handle leaks it, because Shape has no virtual destructor. A vector of unique_ptr<Shape> calls virtual draw on each dynamic object and deletes safely through Shape because its destructor is virtual. In this lesson you'll implement and trace runtime dispatch through a small abstract interface.

```predict
{"question": "Shape::draw is NOT virtual; Circle defines its own draw. Calling draw through a Shape& that refers to a Circle runs...", "options": ["Circle::draw", "Shape::draw: non-virtual calls use the static type"], "answer": 1, "why": "Only virtual functions dispatch on the dynamic type."}
```

examples.title: Drawing a mixed list of shapes
examples.situation: A vector of unique_ptr<Shape> calls virtual draw on each dynamic object and deletes safely through Shape because its destructor is virtual.
walkthrough: **A vector of unique_ptr<Shape>:** holds a Circle and a Square.
**Calls virtual draw on each dynamic object:** the loop prints circle, then square.
**Deletes safely through Shape because its destructor is virtual:** when shapes is destroyed, ~Circle and ~Square will both run.
examples.result: Each shape draws itself correctly and cleans up completely.

examples.title: The typo that didn't override
examples.situation: A Triangle defines `void Draw() const` (capital D). Triangles print nothing special.
walkthrough: Draw is a new function; draw is still the base version.
Adding override makes the compiler report the mistake immediately.
Rename to draw and keep override.
examples.result: Triangles draw themselves, and future typos fail to compile.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Any same-named derived function is dynamically selected even when the base function is not virtual or the object was copied by value.
misconceptions.correction: Dynamic dispatch needs a virtual base function and a call through a reference or pointer. Non-virtual calls and calls on by-value copies use the static type.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, which draw ran and why?

analogy.example: Virtual dispatch is like **a universal remote with a "power" button**. Pressing it (calling draw through Shape) makes **whichever device it's pointed at** respond in its own way. Without virtual, the button is **hard-wired to one device** (Shape) whatever you point it at.
limitations: Remotes need pairing; override is the pairing check.
Unplugging a device properly needs its own shutdown (virtual destructor).

steps.explanation: A vector of unique_ptr<Shape> holds different dynamic types.
It calls virtual draw on each dynamic object at run time.
Deletion through Shape is safe because its destructor is virtual.

trace.textAlternative: Tracing runtime dispatch. Step 1, Store: shapes[0] is Circle; shapes[1] is Square. A vector of unique_ptr<Shape> holds different dynamic types. Step 2, Dispatch: output is circle, square. It calls virtual draw on each dynamic object at run time. Step 3, Delete: destructors is ~Circle, ~Shape, ~Square, ~Shape. Deletion through Shape is safe because its destructor is virtual.

farTransfer.prompt: Design an abstract Notifier interface with send(const std::string&) and implementations EmailNotifier and LogNotifier. Store them in a vector<unique_ptr<Notifier>>, send to all, and use destructor prints to prove complete cleanup. Then remove the virtual destructor and run under -fsanitize=address.

remediation.explanation: For each polymorphic hierarchy check: **virtual on the base function, override on each derived one, a virtual destructor on the base, and calls made through references or pointers.**
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The typo that didn't override".

recap.summary: To implement runtime dispatch, declare base functions virtual (pure virtual for abstract interfaces), mark overrides with override, call through base references or pointers so the dynamic type decides, and give any base that's deleted polymorphically a virtual destructor.
